body.name: In your body
body.desc: Just four elements, O, C, H and N, make up about 96% of your body mass. Tiles show the mass percentage, or grams in a 70 kg person for trace elements.

phone.name: In your phone
phone.desc: EuChemS counts 30 elements in a smartphone. These are the 20 whose supply is a concern. Red: serious threat within 100 years; orange: rising threat from increasing use; yellow: limited availability.

kitchen.name: In the kitchen
kitchen.desc: Elements you meet right in your kitchen: table salt, iodised salt, cast-iron pans, stainless steel pots, foil and tin cans. Sources are on each element's page.

precious.name: Precious
precious.desc: Precious metals: gold, silver and the six platinum-group metals. Rare, durable and almost never rust.

radioactive.name: Radioactive
radioactive.desc: 37 elements have no stable form: every one of their atoms will eventually decay.

liquid.name: Liquid (or almost)
liquid.desc: Mercury and bromine are liquid at room temperature. Gallium, caesium, rubidium and francium melt just a little warmer, below 40 °C.

synthetic.name: Lab-made only
synthetic.desc: The 24 elements from americium (95) onwards do not exist in nature; people make them, usually just a few atoms at a time.

ion.title: Ions
ion.cationRule: Positive ion: the atom loses {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, taken from the outermost shell (highest n) first. That is why transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d, even though 4s fills first.
ion.anionRule: Negative ion: the atom gains {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, which go into the next empty subshell in filling order.
ion.none: This element has no oxidation states in the data.

formulaError.unexpectedChar: The character “{detail}” can’t be used in a formula.
formulaError.unknownElement: No element has the symbol “{detail}”. Symbols are one capital letter, optionally followed by one lowercase letter.
formulaError.lowercaseElement: Element symbols start with a capital letter, e.g. “{detail}”.
formulaError.unclosedGroup: This group is missing its closing bracket.
formulaError.unexpectedClose: This closing bracket has no matching opening bracket.
formulaError.emptyGroup: There is no element inside the brackets.
formulaError.leadingNumber: A formula can’t start with a number. Coefficients belong in equations (e.g. 2H2O) or after a hydrate dot (CuSO4·5H2O).
formulaError.ambiguousCharge: It’s unclear which digits are the count and which are the charge. Write “{detail}”.
formulaError.missingPart: Part of the formula is missing after the hydrate dot.

balanceError.noArrow: Add an arrow between the two sides: “->”, “→” or “=”.
balanceError.manyArrows: An equation can only have one arrow.
balanceError.emptySide: One side of the equation is empty.
balanceError.emptySpecies: There is an extra “+” with nothing between it and the next “+”.
balanceError.impossible: Can’t be balanced: an element (or the charge) appears on one side only. Check the substances.
balanceError.multiple: There are {nullity} independent ways to balance this: it is usually two reactions combined (e.g. two gases formed at once). Split it into separate equations.
balanceError.wrongSide: {species} seems to be on the wrong side.
balanceError.notParticipating: {species} can’t take part in this reaction (its coefficient is 0).

molar.title: Molar mass
molar.intro: Type a formula to get its molar mass and mass percentages, and convert between grams, moles, particles and gas volume.
molar.help: Type it plainly: H2SO4, Ca(OH)2, CuSO4.5H2O, SO4^2-. No need for subscripts.
molar.ionNote: For ions, the mass of the electrons gained or lost is ignored (it is tiny).
molar.converterNote: n = m / M · N = n × 6.022 × 10²³ · V = n × {vm} L (gases only).

balance.title: Balance equations
balance.intro: Type an unbalanced equation; the answer comes with an electron-balance solution (for redox reactions) and an algebraic one, plus limiting and excess reagents.
balance.help: Separate substances with “ + ”, join the sides with “->”, “→” or “=”. Write ions as Fe3+, SO4^2- and electrons as e-. Coefficients you type are checked.
balance.givenWrong: Your coefficients aren’t right: see the answer above.
balance.noElectron: No electron-balance solution (not a redox reaction, or an oxidation number couldn’t be assigned with certainty). See the algebraic method.
balance.electronTotal: Electrons transferred in the balanced equation: {count}.
balance.electronNote: Multiply so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, put the factors into the equation, then balance the remaining elements. Fractional oxidation numbers (like +8/3 in Fe3O4) are averages.

matrix.step1: Each coefficient is an unknown. Each element (and the charge) gives one conservation equation: left total minus right total equals 0.
matrix.step2: Row-reduce the matrix to reduced row echelon form (rank {rank}).
matrix.step3: Set the free unknown to 1 and solve for the rest:

stoich.hint: Enter amounts of reactants (grams or moles) to find the limiting reagent, what is left over and how much product forms.
stoich.summary: Limiting: {names}. The reaction runs {extent} times in the ratio of the equation.

activity.title: Metal activity series
activity.intro: Metals further left are more reactive than metals to their right. Pick a metal to see what it reacts with.
activity.label: Reactivity series of metals
activity.waterYes: Yes, at room temperature: forms a soluble base and releases H₂ gas.
activity.acidYes: Yes: it is before H, so it displaces hydrogen and releases H₂.
activity.acidNo: No: it is after H, so it can’t displace hydrogen.
activity.saltWater: It reacts with the water first (forming a base), so it doesn’t simply displace other metals from their salt solutions.
activity.saltYes: Displaces the metals after it from their salt solutions: {metals}.
activity.saltNone: Can’t displace any metal in the series.
activity.note: Applies to the common school reactions. Nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid are strong oxidizers and behave differently (they even dissolve Cu and Ag).

flame.why: Heat kicks electrons up to higher energy levels; as they fall back they give off light at the element’s characteristic lines.
